reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews / Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
clinicalPearls: Defined by widespread elongation and tortuosity of large and medium arteries, best appreciated on angiographic imaging
Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC2A10, encoding the glucose transporter GLUT10
Arterial stenoses (particularly of the pulmonary arteries and aorta) coexist with the tortuosity and can cause haemodynamic compromise
There is a real risk of aneurysm formation, arterial dissection and ischaemic events including stroke
Systemic connective-tissue features overlap with other arteriopathies: hyperextensible skin, joint hypermobility, hernias and a marfanoid or dysmorphic facial appearance
Whole-body arterial imaging is central to diagnosis and to planning surveillance

Management is largely supportive with regular vascular surveillance and consideration of blood-pressure-lowering agents; some clinicians use beta-blockade or angiotensin-pathway blockers as in related aortopathies
Prognosis relates chiefly to the severity of vascular stenoses and the risk of dissection or rupture
reference.pathophysiology: Arterial tortuosity syndrome is a heritable connective-tissue arteriopathy caused by loss of function of the glucose transporter GLUT10 (SLC2A10). GLUT10 dysfunction is thought to disturb transforming growth factor beta signalling and the metabolism of the arterial wall, impairing elastic fibre organisation in the tunica media. The weakened, disorganised elastic architecture allows the major arteries to elongate and become abnormally tortuous, and predisposes to focal stenoses, aneurysm formation and dissection. The same connective-tissue disturbance produces the skin, joint and facial features. The vascular fragility and stenoses underlie the risks of ischaemia, stroke and arterial rupture.
additionalDifferentials: Other heritable thoracic aortic disease and connective-tissue arteriopathies
additionalInvestigations: Whole-body magnetic resonance or CT angiography for arterial tortuosity and stenoses
Echocardiography for aortic root, pulmonary arteries and cardiac function
Ophthalmological and skeletal evaluation for connective-tissue features
Baseline and periodic vascular imaging for surveillance
redFlags: Chest, back or abdominal pain suggesting arterial dissection or rupture
New neurological deficit indicating stroke or cerebral ischaemia
Haemodynamically significant arterial or pulmonary artery stenosis
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely and is dominated by the vascular phenotype; severe stenoses, aneurysms and dissection carry significant morbidity and mortality, whereas milder disease with careful surveillance can have a more favourable course.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis when tortuosity is incidental and no dedicated arterial imaging is performed
Attributing connective-tissue features to Marfan or Loeys-Dietz without vascular imaging
Underestimating the risk of dissection in seemingly stable patients
references: GeneReviews / OMIM entry for Arterial Tortuosity Syndrome (SLC2A10)
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Antihypertensive therapy to reduce arterial wall stress, favouring beta-blockers and angiotensin receptor blockers such as losartan for their effect on transforming growth factor beta signalling
Whole-body arterial imaging surveillance with magnetic resonance or CT angiography for aneurysm, stenosis and dissection
Endovascular or surgical repair of haemodynamically significant stenoses, aneurysms or arterial dissection
Activity modification, avoiding isometric straining and contact activities that raise arterial wall stress
Echocardiographic monitoring of the aortic root and pulmonary arteries
Manage the connective-tissue features, including hernia repair, joint protection and ophthalmological review
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive SLC2A10 disorder, with confirmatory testing and family screening
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across clinical genetics, cardiology and vascular surgery
